quick_notes.title: Basic Formula
quick_notes.detail: Distance : Speed × Time. km/h to m/s: Multiply by 5/18. m/s to km/h: Multiply by 18/5.
quick_notes.explanation: Distance is how far something travels, speed is how fast it moves, and time is how long it moves. The basic formula is that distance equals speed multiplied by time, so if you know any two of these you can find the third. Speed can be measured in kilometers per hour, written as km/h, or in meters per second, written as m/s. To convert a speed from km/h to m/s you multiply by 5 over 18, which is the same as 5 divided by 18. To convert from m/s to km/h you multiply by 18 over 5, which is 18 divided by 5.

quick_notes.title: Average Speed
quick_notes.detail: 1. (Total Distance / Total Time). 2. If distances are equal : 2xy / (x+y).
quick_notes.explanation: Average speed is a single number that tells you how fast something is moving overall for a whole trip, even if the speed changed during the trip. To find it, you take the total distance traveled, which is the entire length of the path covered, and divide that by the total time taken to travel that entire path. For example, if a car drives 100 kilometers in 2 hours, its average speed is 100 divided by 2, which equals 50 kilometers per hour. There is a special shortcut formula you can use when a trip has two parts that are exactly the same distance, like going from home to school and then back home. In that case, if you traveled at speed x on the first part and speed y on the second part, the average speed for the whole round trip is calculated as 2 times x times y, divided by x plus y. This formula works because it correctly balances the different amounts of time spent at each speed over the equal distances.

quick_notes.title: Relative Speed
quick_notes.detail: Same direction: Subtract (x-y). Opposite direction : Add (x+y).
quick_notes.explanation: Relative speed is how fast the distance between two moving objects changes. When two objects move in the same direction, their relative speed is found by subtracting the slower speed from the faster speed, so if one object moves at speed x and the other at speed y, the relative speed is x minus y. For example, if a car moves at 60 kilometers per hour and a truck moves at 40 kilometers per hour in the same direction, the car gains on the truck at 20 kilometers per hour. When two objects move toward each other, in opposite directions, their relative speed is found by adding their speeds together, so the relative speed is x plus y. For instance, if two trains approach each other, one at 50 kilometers per hour and the other at 70 kilometers per hour, the distance between them closes at 120 kilometers per hour. This concept helps calculate how long it takes for moving objects to meet or pass each other.

quick_notes.title: Train Problems
quick_notes.detail: Train crossing pole: Distance : Length of train. Train crossing platform : Distance : Length of train + Length of platform.
quick_notes.explanation: When a train passes a fixed object like a pole or a person standing still, the distance the train must travel to completely clear that object is exactly equal to the train's own length. For example, if a train is 200 meters long, it will move 200 meters from the moment its front reaches the pole until its rear passes it. However, when a train crosses a platform, it has to travel a longer distance: the train's own length plus the entire length of the platform. So if the same 200-meter train goes past a 300-meter platform, the total distance covered from the front reaching the start of the platform to the rear leaving the end of the platform is 200 plus 300, which is 500 meters. You can use the formula Speed equals Distance divided by Time to find how long this takes or how fast the train is moving.

quick_notes.title: Boats & Streams
quick_notes.detail: Downstream (with flow) : B + S. Upstream (against flow) : B - S. Speed of Boat B : (D+U)/2. Speed of Stream S : (D-U)/2.
quick_notes.explanation: Boats and Streams is a topic about how a boat moves in a river. The river has a current, which is the flowing water, and we call the speed of that current the Stream Speed (S). When the boat moves in the same direction as the current, that is called Downstream (D), and its total speed is the Boat Speed (B) plus the Stream Speed (S), written as B + S. When the boat moves against the current, that is called Upstream (U), and its total speed is the Boat Speed minus the Stream Speed, written as B - S. To find the Boat Speed alone, you add the Downstream speed and the Upstream speed, then divide by 2, using the formula B = (D + U) / 2. To find the Stream Speed alone, you subtract the Upstream speed from the Downstream speed, then divide by 2, using the formula S = (D - U) / 2.
